overview: Awfat, commonly called Ifat, was a Muslim sultanate whose urban heart lay along the Ethiopian highland escarpment. Archaeology and royal inscriptions distinguish its medieval towns from the later region bearing the same name.

items.text: Nora’s medieval houses used stone rubble with earth mortar and interior wall niches. Pottery survives on some earthen floors.
Urban settlements had congregational and neighborhood mosques. Nora also preserves streets and shared open spaces.
Researchers identified reservoir features in the urban network. Nora yielded unglazed ceramics, imported beads and iron rods possibly connected with currency described in texts.
Inscribed Walasma tombs name members of the ruling community and preserve religious invocations. Four dated tombs fall between 1364 and 1373.

The study places Walasma establishment at Awfat in 1285 and a probable capital shift after 1376. Accounts disagree about later rulers’ dates; the city’s loss of capital status did not immediately end the dynasty.

sources.title: Fauvelle, Hirsch and Chekroun, Awfat archaeology and Walasma necropolis, Annales Islamologiques 51
sources.note: Checked passages and chronology qualifications appear in the accompanying evidence dossier.
